name: Nigeria
summary: Africa’s most populous country, formed as a British colony in 1914 and independent in 1960, with hundreds of ethnic groups.

knownFor.label: Nollywood
knownFor.note: One of the world’s largest film industries.

location.value: West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea; about 924,000 km².

terrain.value: Coastal mangroves, forest and savanna; the Niger and Benue rivers join and flow into the Niger Delta.

climate.value: Tropical; the far south has a rainforest climate with 1,500–2,000 mm of rain a year.

resources.value: Oil and gas, farmland, tin and other minerals.

disasters.value: Floods (notably in 2012 and 2022) and drought in the north.

population.value: More than 242 million, the most populous country in Africa.

urbanisation.value: Lagos is one of the largest metropolitan areas in the world and the second-largest in Africa.

disease.value: Malaria; Nigeria was the first country to contain and eliminate Ebola in the 2014 outbreak.

migration.value: Rapid growth of cities such as Lagos, one of the largest in Africa, and large emigration abroad.

economicBase.value: Oil exports provide most export income, with farming and services employing most people.

tradeRoutes.value: Oil is shipped from the Niger Delta to Europe, India and the Americas.

inequality.value: Very high inequality between a rich elite and many poor people, and between north and south.

governmentType.value: A federal republic of 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (Abuja); military dictatorships after the civil war, stable democracy since 1999.

keyRulers.value: Nnamdi Azikiwe. Obafemi Awolowo. Later and present leaders are not named here.

stability.value: Civil war (1967–70); the Boko Haram insurgency, including the Chibok schoolgirls kidnapping (2014).

eliteConflict.value: Regional and ethnic rivalries, including the civil war over Biafra (1967–70), still shape politics.

armyAndTech.value: One of Africa’s largest armies, which ruled the country for much of 1966–99.

territoryChange.value: Nigeria lost Bakassi to Cameroon after a 2002 court ruling and the 2008 handover.

alliancesRivals.value: Helped found ECOWAS (1975) and leads regional integration in West Africa.

inventions.value: Fintech and mobile money services have grown rapidly since the 2010s.

scienceEducation.value: Wole Soyinka won the Nobel Prize in Literature (1986).

openness.value: Open to trade and migration, with a lively press.

communicationTransport.value: Roads carry most traffic; the Lagos–Ibadan railway opened in 2021.

religion.value: About half Muslim (mostly north), half Christian (mostly south).

languageWriting.value: English is the official language; the Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo make up over 60% of the people, alongside hundreds of other groups.

artsArchitecture.value: Nollywood, the world’s second-largest film producer by number; Afrobeat music; the medieval art of Ife.

socialStructure.value: More than 250 ethnic groups, led by the Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba and Igbo, and wide gaps between rich and poor.

sharedIdentity.value: Ethnic, regional and religious identities remain strong, alongside a growing national culture of film and music.

dailyLife.value: City flats and village compounds; jollof rice, yams.

ideasReligions.value: Pan-Africanism: support for liberation movements in Angola, Namibia and elsewhere in the 1970s.

colonisation.value: Formed by Britain, which merged the Southern and Northern Nigeria Protectorates in 1914; independent in 1960.

peakPeriod.value: The 1970s oil boom, when Nigeria joined OPEC.

declineSignals.value: Corruption, insecurity and conflict hold back growth.

outcome.value: Nigeria continues as an independent federal republic.
